reference_opening.argument: The video presents Gate.io and a linked workshop as routes to make substantial money, generate large commissions, and multiply wealth through cryptocurrency. The speaker directly asks viewers to follow an external link and submit an email address for that workshop, connecting the earnings framing to the video's own lead-generation solicitation. Although the speaker acknowledges investment risk and warns against guaranteed-return Ponzi-style offers, those warnings do not verify the promoted workshop's contents, costs, data handling, or earnings outcomes.

opening.argument: The speaker repeatedly frames crypto as a risk-bearing investment rather than a guaranteed-income scheme. He expressly says the market may rise, fall, or remain flat, warns that a crash may prevent withdrawal, and rejects offers promising fixed returns. He also tells viewers to do their homework and distinguishes ordinary exchange use from Ponzi-style MLM deals. That is materially inconsistent with deceptive certainty: the discussion presents conditional possibilities and personal risk, not a promise that viewers will profit.

citations.quote: nobody can guarantee you returns
the market may go up it may go down and make or flat
if the markets crash and they crash all the time because that's what crypto is like you might not be able to withdraw your money
you just need to do your homework

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution emphasizes wealth language and the workshop link, but it omits the unusually direct risk qualification. The speaker specifically tells viewers that crypto can crash, withdrawal may become impossible, and guaranteed-return offers should be avoided. The existence of an invitation to educational material does not transform every conditional investment discussion into a guarantee or establish that the workshop promises a particular outcome.

citations.quote: stay away from MLM crypto deals and stuff that guarantee returns
crypto even though it's doing really really well right um it's a risk it's an investment

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Risk language does not erase the promotional message. The speaker still says viewers can buy and hold tokens for three, five, or ten years to grow wealth exponentially, then directs them to a workshop. Saying returns are not guaranteed may acknowledge volatility, but it does not substantiate the implied wealth-building outcome or the workshop's contents.

opening.argument: The presentation is structured as a review and tutorial: it explains how an exchange works, describes spot trading and other products, compares platforms, and demonstrates where rewards and campaigns appear. The title itself calls it a review and tutorial, while the description says viewers will learn how the exchange works and whether it is legitimate. The speaker also warns against specific third-party schemes, making the overall format instructional and evaluative rather than a simple demand to send money.

citations.quote: Gate.io Review - Tutorial To Show You How To Make Big Money With This Crypto Exchange!
gate.io review and tutorial
I would stick to the spot trade
I'm gonna show you a couple of coins and a couple of deals that I called out in my reviews

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling something a tutorial does not settle its function, but the actual content supports the instructional reading: it explains spot trading, contrasts it with derivatives, and warns viewers away from guaranteed-return schemes. The prosecution's focus on the workshop treats a closing educational invitation as proof of a scam without showing that the lesson is fabricated, paid, or tied to a required deposit.

citations.quote: they also have more advanced you know derivatives
anything that looks like that, you want to stay away from that

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The tutorial framing does not make the promotion neutral. The speaker connects the exchange lesson to his own claimed wealth-building method, says he teaches that method in training courses, and directs viewers to enter an email for a workshop. Those solicitation elements remain even if the video also contains operational explanations.

citations.quote: I teach this inside a lot of my training courses
on the next page enter your best email address
connect them to people that want those products

opening.argument: The observable mechanism is ordinary exchange use and affiliate-style commerce: a viewer may use a cryptocurrency platform, buy or hold an asset, or learn how the speaker sells digital products for commissions. The speaker does not instruct viewers to recruit a downline, deposit money into his control, or accept a guaranteed return. He explicitly describes the exchange as a place to buy and trade crypto and characterizes his own income as a commission for connecting customers with products. Even the displayed earnings and payout pages show interfaces, not proof that viewers are asked to fund the speaker or that a payout must be purchased.

citations.quote: you would be able to basically buy cryptocurrency
I become a middle person
when they buy the product, I make a commission directly from these companies

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution identifies a link and email collection, but those are compatible with an ordinary free workshop or lead-generation funnel and do not establish a required payment, credential misuse, downline, or guaranteed return. The cited wealth language describes what the speaker says he does with commissions; it does not show that viewers must transfer funds to him or that the exchange guarantees appreciation.

citations.quote: Jump on to my free workshop
I make a commission directly from these companies

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The missing scam mechanism is not decisive when the video promotes token purchase and holding as a wealth-growth route. The speaker says to buy crypto through Gate.io, hold it, and later use the resulting income strategy to multiply wealth, while the workshop is the conversion path. The payout screen and commission explanation demonstrate persuasive earnings framing, even if they do not prove a deposit or guaranteed payout.
